Text One: What is Endometriosis?

In women with endometriosis, the endometrial cells that normally line the uterus
attach themselves and grow on different organs outside the uterus, such as the
fallopian tubes, ovaries, bladder and bowel. This endometrial tissue goes through
the same process of thickening and bleeding-that occurs during menstruation, but
has no way of leaving the body. The trapped endometrial tissue can cause_pain,
swelling and bleeding in the area of the tissue. Severe pain and heavy or irregular
bleeding are the most common symptoms. <—
Endometriosis is a common condition that affects up to 10% of women reproductive
age. However, true prevalence is unknown because many women are
asymptomatic.

Endometriosis is more commonly found in white women than in Black and Asian
women, and in tall, thin women with a low body mass index. Delaying pregnancy
until later in life is also believed to be a risk factor. The risk of endometriosis is
reported to be higher among women with moles, freckles and skin that burns easily.

Although the cause of endometriosis is unknown, the most common theory is that
\endometrial tissue is éposited in unusual locations when menstrual flow is backed
up.into the fallopiantubes and the pelvic and abdominal cavity.during menstruation
(retrograde menstruation). Many women have retrograde menstruation in varying
_degrees, but not all of them develop endometriosis. Recent research in Australia
indicates that the endometrial tissue of women who develop endometriosis differs
from that of non-affected women although it is unknown whether the cause is genetic
or environmental or both.
Endometriosis is diagnosed using Laparoscopy to obtain biopsy samples. There is
no cure for endometriosis. Treatment focuses on reducing pain through the use of
anti-inflammatory drugs and pain relievers and shrinking the endometrial tissue
through hormonal treatment, which unfortunately can create a range of side effects.
Laparoscopic surgery can be used to remove or destroy endometrial tissue, but the
tissue usually grows back in time. Only a full hysterectomy can fully end severe
_cases of endometriosis.

Women with endometriosis have a mildly increased risk for development of certain
types of cancer of the ovary, known as epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC). This risk
seems to-be highest in women with endometriosis-and-primary infertility (those who
have-never borne a child), but the use of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), which are
sometimes used ‘in the treatment of endometriosis, appears to significantly reduce
this risk.

are not clearly understood. One theory is that the endometriosis implants themselves

>One in five women with infertility suffers from endometriosis. However, the condition
isually does not fully prevent conception. Most women with endometriosis will still be
able to conceive, especially those with mild to moderate endometriosis. It is
estimated that up to(70%/of women with mild and moderate endometriosis will
conceive within three years \ without any specific treatment:

The reasons for a decrease in fertility are not completely understood, but might be
due to both. arratomic and_hormonal factors. “The presence of endometriosis may
involve masses of tissue or scarring-(adhesions) within the pelvis that may distort
normal anatomical structures, such as Fallopian tubes, which transport the eggs
from the ovaries. Alternatively, endometriosis may affect fertility through the
production of hormones and other substances that have a negative effect on
ovulation, fertilization of the egg, and/or implantation of the embryo. Infertility
associated with endometriosis is more common in women with severe forms of the
disease.

Treatment options for infertility associated with endometriosis are-varied,but most
doctors believe that surgical tr¢atments-are-superior_to hofmonal-or medical
treatments for endometriosis when the goal is enhancement of fertility. Assisted
reproduction techniques may.also.be used when appropriate in combination with
surgical therapy.

Text 4: Recent Research finds Endometriosis in the ovaries doubles the risk of
premature birth

A comparative study of over 6,000 births, led by Professor David Healy, Director of
the Jean Hailes Foundation for Women’s Health and Chairman of the Monash
University Department_of Obstetrics-and_Gynaecology, found that women who had
used assisted reproductive technologies to conceive, and who had ovarian
endometriosis, are twice as likely to have a premature birth.

Further research is needed to determine the clinical benefit of.removing the ovarian
endometriosis prior:to using any assisted reproductive technologies and to address
the gaps in our understanding of the ‘chain of events leading from ovarian
endometriosis to premature birth.

“This research is important for.all pregnant women and is the first time that
endometriosis has been so clearly associated with premature birth,” Professor Healy
said. “Obstetricians will now be able to more readily identify and monitor meget: to-
be who are at increased risk of premature labour and birth.”

Clinicans looking after women who have conceived using assisted reproductive .
technologies will now be able to check for ovarian endometriosis through routine
ultrasound: Diagnosed: women.can then be monitored throughout their pregnancy.
According to Prof Healy, the key will be early diagnosis, “especially as up to 44 per
cent of women show no symptoms of endometriosis.”
